title: Orthodox Judaism
hookLine: holds the Torah as divinely given and halakha as binding

lines: NOT A NICE IDEA. THE LAW.
cards: An apple on a kitchen counter. A teenager grabs it on the way out the door, already late, phone in the other hand. Before the first bite, she stops.
A few Hebrew words under her breath, a blessing for the fruit of the tree, and then the crunch. It takes about as long as a red light. Nobody is watching.
She says it anyway, because in her home that pause is not a nice idea. It is the law, and the law is binding, the same as on any other morning.

teach.h: TORAH FROM HEAVEN, WRITTEN AND ORAL.
teach.b: Orthodox Judaism. Take yesterday's three questions and hear its answers. First, revelation.

Orthodox Jews hold that the Torah is from heaven: given by God to Moses. And not only the written scroll. An oral teaching came with it, explaining how to live the written words, and it was handed down.

The Mishnah's tractate of the Fathers opens with that chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly.
Because the source is divine, the law is binding. Shabbat, the dietary laws, prayer, blessings like the teenager's: these are commandments, kept today as they were kept before.
Deuteronomy says: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it." Third, change. Orthodoxy doesn't say nothing ever changes.
New questions arrive constantly: an elevator on Shabbat, a new medicine, a new food additive.
A trained rabbi answers them from inside the law, reasoning from the Talmud, the codes like the Shulchan Aruch, and the rulings of earlier scholars. The answer can be new.
The method and the authority stay within the tradition. Fourth, Orthodoxy is not one community.
Soon you'll meet several streams inside it, each with its own style.

teach.h: YE SHALL NOT ADD, NEITHER DIMINISH.
teach.b: What holds them together is today's line. For Orthodox Jews, the tradition isn't something they own. It binds them, and they are bound to it.

how: Orthodox Jews keep halakha as binding, including Shabbat, kashrut, daily prayer and blessings before and after eating, and bring new questions to rabbis who answer from the Talmud, the codes and earlier rulings.

o: a Jewish branch of the Eastern Orthodox churches
any Jewish group that prays mostly in Hebrew
the movement holding Torah from God and law as binding

p: the Torah, written and oral, from God
Moses received the Torah at Sinai

s: Orthodox Judaism says nothing can ever be asked anew

Orthodox Jews hold that an oral teaching came with the written Torah
and it was handed down: Moses to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets, to the sages.
Orthodoxy is a single community with one style

games.q: you're the teenager, late, apple in hand, nobody watching. what do you do?
o: skip the blessing; nobody will know.
stop and say the blessing, then bite.
games.why: she says it anyway. in her home the pause is not a nice idea; it is the law, binding whether or not anyone sees.

practice: If there's a cup of water or something to eat nearby, set it in front of you, or picture it, and before you take it, stop and notice the urge to reach. Notice where it came from, the hands and the rain behind it.
If you pray, say a blessing you already know; if not, let the pause stand for a few breaths, then drink or eat slowly.

wordCard.voice: Orthodox Judaism. The movement that holds the Torah, written and oral, as given by God, and halakha as binding, with new questions answered from inside the law. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: halakha, Jewish law, which Orthodox Judaism holds as binding.

carryVoice: Your line: binding tradition. Three seconds before a bite can hold a whole way of life. Back tomorrow, same hill.
